learningObjective: Identify the benefits and costs of function inlining and the conditions when it may be inhibited.
stem: Which statements about function inlining as a compiler optimization are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Recursive functions cannot be inlined at all; the compiler always emits them as separate call sites.
Indirect / virtual calls typically require devirtualization (via type information or profiling) before they can be inlined, since the target is not statically known.
Inlining eliminates the call/return overhead and enables intraprocedural optimizations (constant propagation, CSE, LICM) to see across the previous call boundary.

Aggressive inlining can hurt performance by inflating instruction cache footprint (icache misses), increasing register pressure, and slowing compile time; heuristics balance size and estimated benefit.

explanation: A: canonical benefit of inlining. B: canonical cost — icache pressure, register pressure, compile-time bloat. D: indirect calls need devirtualization (or PGO-guided speculative inlining) before they can be inlined. C is wrong: recursive functions CAN be inlined up to a bound (e.g., partial recursion unrolling for tail-recursive or bounded-depth cases); however, unbounded recursion prevents full inlining.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: bounded inlining of recursion is possible; unbounded is not.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: indirect calls need devirtualization first.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: canonical costs; heuristics balance them.

assumptions: Standard compiler with an inlining heuristic (size/benefit model).
nonImplications: Does not imply -O3 always inlines aggressively; heuristics may limit inlining based on caller/callee size.
Does not imply all indirect calls are irrecoverable; profiling and type-based devirtualization can convert many into direct calls.
